         STAFF’S EXCEPTIONS TO THE CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION

           COMES NOW the Utility Division Staff (“Staff”) of the New Mexico Public

Regulation Commission (“Commission”) and, under 1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC and, to the

extent applicable, 1.2.2.37(C) NMAC, files these Exceptions to the Hearing Examiners’

Certification of Stipulation issued October 23, 2026 (“Certification” or “Cert.”). 1

           The Exceptions are organized in four parts: (I) the Certification’s misstatement of

Staff’s position and of the burden of proof (Exceptions 1–2); (II) future test year (“FTY”)

forecast and linkage data (Exceptions 3–5); (III) jurisdictional allocation (Exceptions 6–

7); and (IV) bill impacts, affordability, and the public-interest determination (Exception 8).

Unless an Exception states otherwise, each is taken to the extent the cited paragraphs

support Findings (9)(a), (10) and (11) and Decretal ¶¶ (A)–(C) and (E) adopting the $90

million revenue requirement in Section 1.1. Exception 8 also concerns Finding (9)(e)

(Section 1.11). Citations to the Certification are to paragraph and printed page (“Page X of

156”). “IB” is Staff’s Post-Hearing Brief (Aug. 14, 2026); “RB” is Staff’s Post-Hearing

Response Brief (Aug. 31, 2026).



I. THE CERTIFICATION MISSTATES STAFF’S POSITION AS A REQUEST
FOR A HISTORICAL TEST PERIOD AND SHIFTS THE BURDEN OF PROVING
COMPLIANCE WITH SECTION 62-6-14 (D) FROM SPS TO STAFF

Exception No. 1 — The Certification recasts Staff’s position as a demand for a
historical test period (Cert. ¶¶ 61, 86–93).
       Staff takes exception to the Certification’s statement that “the largest driver of

Staff’s recommendation is that SPS must use a historical test period.” Cert. ¶ 61 (p. 27).


1
    The Exceptions are timely filed within ten days after certification. 1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC

       Docket No. 25-00079-UT
       Staff’s Exceptions
       Page 5 of 25
 Staff also takes exception to ¶ 86 (Staff contends the best period “is the historical test

period”), ¶ 87 (Staff “elides the last sentence of Section 62-6-14(D)”), ¶ 90 (Staff “does

not provide an argument” on why the FTY is not the best period), and ¶ 92 (Staff

“undermines its argument” by accepting the FTY for New Mexico-specific items), and to

¶¶ 89, 91 and 93 to the extent they rest on those characterizations.


           These paragraphs should not be adopted for three reasons. First, they describe a

position Staff did not take. Second, they treat NMSA 1978, § 62-6-14(D), which pertains

to the future test period, as if it answered whether SPS proved the forecast inputs within

that period, governed by § 62-8-7(A). Third, the Certification applies Commission’s FTY

Rule 17.1.3.14 NMAC, entitled SUPPORTING TESTIMONY AND EXHIBITS

REQUIRED: “The required data shall be accompanied by testimony and exhibits

explaining and justifying quantities, assumptions, expectations, activity changes, etc. and

verifying that the amounts used to support the future test year period are the utility's most

recently available data.”at ¶ 140 yet does not explain why it does not apply here.


A. Staff challenged the proof within the FTY and did 2 not the FTY itself.

           Staff’s position was that SPS had not shown that its “material forecasted expenses,

rate-base additions, revenues, load, allocators and other cost-of-service inputs are

sufficiently supported to represent expected conditions when new rates will be in effect.”

IB 12 (quoted at Cert. ¶ 84). Staff stated that “[t]he Commission may continue to use a

FTY for New Mexico-specific costs, revenues, and other properly supported FTY



2
    Direct Testimony Dr. Larry Blank.

      Docket No. 25-00079-UT
      Staff’s Exceptions
      Page 6 of 25
 adjustments” (IB 27, quoted at Cert. ¶ 86) and that its recommendation “does not require

the Commission to abandon the FTY” (IB 30). Dr. Blank proposed base-year 12-CP and

energy values “for the sole purpose of separating the revenue requirement between the

Texas, New Mexico, and the FERC wholesale jurisdictions.” Cert. ¶ 66 (quoting Blank

Direct at 9–10).


           The utility bears “the burden of proof to show that the increased rate or charge is

just and reasonable.” NMSA 1978, § 62-8-7(A). Arguing that SPS failed to carry that

burden for particular future test year inputs challenges the evidence, not the future test

period itself. Staff witness Blank’s allocator proposal is a remedy for SPS’s future test

year invalid inputs. The Cert. ¶ 89 discussed IB 12) and rejected Staff’s overriding

conclusion that SPS’s forecasts “do[] not comport with Section 62-6-14(D),” and therefore

do not best reflect the conditions at the time the rates will take effect. However, Staff

argued 3 that SPS must use actual, non-speculative data) and SPS must adjust for the Texas

New Mexico mismatch in order to fairly divide the shared system costs. The Certification

rejected Staff’s criticism of SPS’s forecasted inputs within the FTY by simply stating that

it was legal for SPS to overrecover. However, the Certification did not analyze howthat

does not violate Section 62-6-14 (D) and the fair, just and reasonable standard in Section

62-8-7 (A).


B. Staff did not “elide” § 62-6-14(D) and made the comparative argument the
Certification says is missing.



3
    IB 12; IB 27 and IB 30 must be read together.

      Docket No. 25-00079-UT
      Staff’s Exceptions
      Page 7 of 25
        Staff’s Response Brief quoted § 62-6-14(D) in full, including the “due

consideration” sentence, and conceded that the statute “does not require the applicant to

continuously update every future-test-year assumption.” (RB 4–5). Staff argued that due

consideration means the Commission must determine what “best reflects” the conditions

at the time the rate will take effect.     Due consideration imposes “a duty upon the

Commission to compare and decide if the FTY rates best reflect the conditions at the time

the rates will go into effect.” RB 13. Staff applied that due consideration by comparing

jurisdictional allocators in Texas and New Mexico: SPS’s allocators assume 524 MW of

New Mexico production-demand growth against 174 MW for Texas (RB 13, citing Blank

Direct at 10) and were not updated during the case (RB 5–6).


       “Due consideration” that a future period “may” best reflect rate-effective conditions

creates no presumption that each future test year forecast input within it’s FTY application

is accurate, and nothing in § 62-6-14(D) relieves SPS from the burden under § 62-8-7(A).

Staff did not elide the statute. Staff addressed the Commission’s due consideration relative

to the utility’s ultimate burden. Staff is not saying that SPS does not have a statutory right

to choose a future test year and should file a historic test year. Rather Staff is saying

specific SPS FTY inputs within the FTY are deficient and invalid.


C. The Certification is inconsistent in its application of the Commission FTY Rule
17.1.3.14 NMAC for supporting testimony and exhibits and 17.1.3.17 NMAC

       The Certification states that the FTY Supporting Testimony and Exhibit Rule

17.1.3.14 Staff cited “simply establish the standards for the data that must be presented.”

Cert. ¶ 87. The Certification correctly applied this Rule and disallowed $265,322 of FTY

   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 8 of 25
 Community Solar Portal O&M agreeing with Staff that SPS did not provide the testimony

and exhibits the FTY Rule 17.1.3.17 requires (Cert. ¶ 140), and it reduced FTY rate-case

expense on the record evidence (Cert. ¶¶ 236–247). However, it did not apply this same

Rule to the financial load forecast, resource adequacy inputs and jurisdictional allocators.

Data that does not meet the standards of 17.1.3.17 NMAC cannot carry SPS’s burden under

§ 62-8-7(A) in any test period, historical or future. Staff asks for the same treatment for the

financial load forecast, the resource-adequacy inputs and the jurisdictional allocators.

There is no “contradiction” as asserted in the Certification ¶ 92 by Staff recommending the

Commission use historical inputs within the future test year for purposes of jurisdictional

division of shared system resources. Nor is there a contradiction in Staff requesting the

Commission disallow recovery of a stale revenue requirement where SPS did not provide

supporting testimony and exhibits, particularly where future test year inputs are not

adequately explained or supported and there are material changes. 4 That is the approach

the Certification itself took to disallow the Community Solar Portal expenses. The

Commission should apply the FTY Rules to all future test year inputs, not pick and choose.


Exception No. 2 — The Certification resolves the FTY and allocation issues by
shifting the burden of proof from SPS to Staff (Cert. ¶¶ 82, 90, 93, 127–130, 142).
        Staff takes exception to dispositive findings phrased in terms of Staff’s failure of

proof: that Staff “has not explained how SPS’s selection of a future test period for

jurisdictional allocation has been based on projected or speculative load growth alone” (¶

82); that Staff “does not provide an argument” (¶ 90); that Staff “does not establish a basis



4
    17.1.3.17 (A) NMAC.

      Docket No. 25-00079-UT
      Staff’s Exceptions
      Page 9 of 25
 for concluding that the future test period selected by SPS is not the time period that best

reflects” rate-effective conditions (¶ 93); and that Staff “has not established” a violation of

New Mexico law or the 25-00066-UT Final Order “or that a historical test period would

better reflect the conditions” (¶ 142). Staff also takes exception to the finding that “it is

possible that the updated revenue deficiency became known after” March 20, 2026, and

the conclusion that SPS “was not required to provide updated data” (¶¶ 129–130).

        These portions should not be adopted because, at the points that decide the outcome,

the Certification asks the wrong party to prove its case, and it resolves record gaps about

timing in SPS’s favor although it applies the opposite rule at ¶ 238.

A. The Certification states the correct burden of proof but then shifts it to apply to
Staff.
       The Certification correctly holds that SPS bears the burden under § 62-8-7(A) and

the Signatories under 1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC. Cert. ¶¶ 25, 34–35. Staff argued that it “does

not need to establish that SPS has already obtained a specific 105% recovery . . . . SPS

bears the burden of proof, not Staff.” RB 11. A finding that the opponent “has not

established” a defect is not a finding that the proponent carried its burden. The question is

whether SPS and the Signatories proved, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the

forecasted inputs and allocators and the resulting $90 million produce just and reasonable

rates. Cert. ¶ 35. At ¶ 82 the question is whether SPS proved its allocators rest on more

than load growth. At ¶¶ 93 and 142 it is whether SPS proved its allocators reflect rate-

effective conditions, not whether Staff proved a historical period is better.             More

importantly, Staff is not arguing for a historical test period. Staff is arguing for a validated

and verified future test period.


   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 10 of 25
 B. Gaps about timing should count against SPS.

       The Certification called “[t]he crux of the matter” when SPS knew of the updated

information and whether it would cause a material revision (Cert. ¶ 127), then found the

record does not show when SPS knew, and that CBH-18 does not show the date of the

discovery response (¶¶ 128–129). That is not the crux of the matter, which instead is

whether SPS complied with the FTY Rule by failing to verify with the updated information.

Nevertheless, the response was SPS’s answer to Staff RFI 3-75 (Tr. Vol. III at 593:12–13),

attached to testimony filed May 1, 2026 (Cert. ¶ 128). At ¶ 238, the Certification rejected

SPS’s argument that Staff should have attached discovery responses as “flip[ping] the

burden in this case on its head,” and noted that SPS could have submitted more detailed

information under 17.1.3.19(D) NMAC. When facts that decide an issue are missing, the

gap counts against the party with the burden. § 62-8-7(A); 1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC; Int’l

Minerals, 81 N.M. at 283 (cited at Cert. ¶ 34 n.58). A finding that a favorable fact is

“possible” (¶ 129) is not a finding that SPS proved it. Only SPS knew when its data

changed, so only SPS could put that date in the record.

II. FTY FORECAST AND LINKAGE DATA


Exception No. 3 — The Certification adopts the right linkage standard but does not
apply it (Cert. ¶¶ 99, 101, 134).
       Staff takes exception to the failure to apply the standard adopted at ¶¶ 99 and 101:

a linkage period beginning before the filing date “should certainly contain actual numbers

that are available at the time of filing,” and SPS “should have been able to provide up-to-

date actual numbers for data that was available prior to November 20, 2025.” Staff does

not take exception to the standard. It takes exception because the Certification never applies

   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 11 of 25
 it to the pre-filing months, and the only record evidence on those months shows SPS did

not meet it.

       The linkage period runs from July 1, 2025 through November 30, 2026; SPS filed

on November 20, 2025. Application at 2; Cert. ¶ 101. SPS describes its linkage data as

“based on known and measurable cost adjustments.” Lees Direct at 17–18. Dr. Blank

testified: “SPS has provided this Linkage data. The problem with the Linkage data in this

record is that was also Forecasted. It is not based on actuals, nor was it updated.” Tr. Vol.

IV at 784:17–20; see also id. at 785:3–6. After announcing its standard, the Certification

turns entirely to post-filing updates. Cert. ¶¶ 100–133. Footnote 185 treats Dr. Blank as

suggesting a future rule improvement, but that suggestion concerned updates as a case

proceeds. Tr. Vol. IV at 784:21–25.

       Linkage data creates “a verifiable link between future test year period data and base

period data … for the purpose of validating the information contained in the future test year

period.” 17.1.3.7(H) NMAC (quoted at Cert. ¶ 96). Forecasts for months that had already

passed at filing cannot validate the FTY against actuals. Under the Certification’s own

standard that is a present deficiency, not a topic for future rulemaking.

Requested modification.

       Add a finding that SPS did not show that its linkage data for July 1, 2025 through

the filing date reflected the actual data available when it filed, as ¶¶ 99 and 101 require,

and revise ¶ 134 accordingly.




   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 12 of 25
 Exception No. 4 — Revisions SPS disclosed in discovery and at the public hearing
had to be reconciled (Cert. ¶¶ 131–132).
       Staff takes exception to the statement that “17.1.3.19 NMAC is permissive as to

whether the utility chooses to inform the Commission, Staff, and intervenors of revisions

that are not errors” (¶ 131) and the conclusion that “there is no requirement in 17.1.3

NMAC that requires updates to data that becomes known through discovery responses that

are filed after the date on which the comprehensive list of revisions is filed” (¶ 132).

These paragraphs should not be adopted for three reasons. First, 17.1.3.19(C) NMAC ties

the duty to reconcile and update to the revision, not to the date the list is due. Second, ¶

132 (no requirement to update changes after the list is filed) conflicts with the

Certification’s holding at ¶ 107 that linkage data must remain verifiable (filing revisions to

linkage data is “structurally implied”). Third, even a permissive update FTY Rule does not

relieve SPS of its burden to prove its application is valid under Section 62-8-7 (A).

A. The reconciliation obligation attaches to the revision.

       SPS disclosed the changed deficiency in a response to Staff discovery and at the

public hearing: from 77 MW to 45 MW, plus 176 MW of expected interruptible

participation. Tr. Vol. III at 593:12–13; 594:16–25. The change was not on SPS’s March

20, 2026 Comprehensive List (Cert. ¶ 128), and SPS filed no reconciliation against its FTY

revenue requirement or allocators (Tr. Vol. III at 595:16–18; Cert. ¶ 126). Under

17.1.3.19(C) NMAC, “[r]evisions provided by the utility … in response to discovery

requests that do not require the filing of a modification by the utility shall be incorporated

into a comprehensive list,” presented “as adjustments to the utility’s original presentation

… so that the adjustments are verifiable.” (Quoted at Cert. ¶ 102.) The Procedural Order

   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 13 of 25
 schedule controls when the list is filed; it does not exempt SPS from reconciling later

revisions.

B. The changes in the forecasted data were material and SPS was required to

reconcile and revise to ensure their rates were fair, just and reasonable..

       SPS’s revisions are material enough to trigger 17.1.3.19 reconciliation because the

facts already in the record total about $7.80 million: $3,054,395 from the Comprehensive

List (Cert. ¶ 38) and $4,749,000 from the depreciation correction (Cert. ¶ 113). Five percent

of the originally filed deficiency of $175,354,544 (Cert. ¶¶ 37–38) is about $8.77 million,

so an unquantified change of roughly $1 million or more would cross that line if materiality

is measured cumulatively. SPS cannot benefit from its failure to do so because only SPS

could calculate that effect,. § 62-8-7(A).

       The Certification argues Subsection D as permitting post-list updates (¶ 104). Staff

disagrees and SPS did not use argue that. (Tr. Vol. III at 595:16–18; Cert. ¶ 126). Even if

Subsection D is permissive, SPS bears the evidentiary consequences of that choice. Cf.

Cert. ¶ 238.

Exception No. 5 — The Certification finds the data stale, yet approves rates built
upon it (Cert. ¶¶ 126, 133–134).
       Staff takes exception to the conclusion that Staff’s linkage-data arguments “both

fail.” Cert. ¶ 134. That conclusion follows the Hearing Examiners’ findings that “the data

that is being considered in this case, both for the resource deficiency and for the financial

load forecast, is stale,” that “stale data [is] the basis for the decisions made in this matter”

(¶ 133), and that SPS “did not provide the Commission with updated data that was in its




   Docket No. 25-00079-UT
   Staff’s Exceptions
   Page 14 of 25
 possession” (¶ 126). Staff takes exception to ¶¶ 126 and 133 to the extent they are treated

as having no consequence for the revenue requirement.


          ¶ 134 should not be adopted for two reasons and the Commission should accept

Staff’s linkage data deficiency arguments. First, the Certification asks only whether the

FTY rule required SPS to update, or was only allowed and not whether SPS carried its

burden to fulfill the standard of fair, just and reasonable rates with data found stale. Second,

a forecast found stale cannot be presumed to “best reflect” conditions when rates take

effect.


A. SPS did not comply with the update rule and does not establish that SPS carried

its burden to prove the rates are fair, just and reasonable.

          Mr. Gable’s direct testimony identified a 77 MW capacity shortfall for 2026–2027.

Tr. Vol. III at 591:22–25. At hearing he said SPS had secured a short-term capacity

purchase, that outages, resource unavailability and updated load forecasts “can change,”

and that “those numbers have been updated.” Id. at 592:3–15. He also said: “I do not know

that we have updated the Financial Forecast since this Testimony filing,” and

acknowledged that SPS’s response to Staff RFI 3-75 “indicates that we have not updated

the Financial Forecast.” Id. at 592:19–20; 593:12–15. SPS’s discovery response projected

a 45 MW deficiency with 176 MW of interruptible support; Mr. Gable testified this “hasn’t

been updated or provided,” was not final and was expected to change, and was “a little bit

dated” because the “’26 V1 Financial Forecast has been completed.” Id. at 594:21–25;

595:16–25; 596:1–2; 596:16–20. SPS also stated in discovery that it “has not prepared an


    Docket No. 25-00079-UT
    Staff’s Exceptions
    Page 15 of 25
 update to the financial load forecast since the initial identification of the likely deficiency.”

Cert. ¶ 133 n.184 (citing NMLCG Hrg. Ex. 3, Att. CBH-18 at 20).


        The Certification then asks only whether 17.1.3 NMAC required an update or did

SPS have permission not to update. Cert. ¶¶ 127–133. Complying with 17.1.3.19 NMAC

is a separate question from carrying the burden under § 62-8-7(A); a utility can follow

every procedural step and still fail to prove its case. Before approving the Stipulation, the

Commission must decide whether SPS proved that the financial load forecast and resource-

adequacy inputs support just and reasonable rates under §§ 62-8-1 and 62-8-7(A).

1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC.


B. A stale forecast cannot be presumed to “best reflect” rate-effective conditions.

        Mr. Gable, the sponsoring witness, said the figures had changed and would change

again (Tr. Vol. III at 592:3–15; 595:16–25; 596:1–2), and the Hearing Examiners found

the forecast stale (¶ 133). Section 62-6-14(D) asks which period “best reflects” rate-

effective conditions (Cert. ¶ 88). Without evidence from SPS, a stale forecast cannot be

presumed to meet that standard. The principle that the result controls over the method (Cert.

¶ 22) still requires a reasoned finding that the result is reasonable on this record, and the

Certification makes none that accounts for its own staleness finding.


Requested modification.

        Add to ¶ 133 a finding that SPS has not carried its burden under § 62-8-7(A) to

show that the financial load forecast, and the resource-adequacy inputs that depend on it,

reflect conditions expected when rates take effect on December 1, 2026.


    Docket No. 25-00079-UT
    Staff’s Exceptions
    Page 16 of 25
 III. JURISDICTIONAL ALLOCATION


Exception No. 6 — The Certification mischaracterizes Staff’s reliance on the Case
No. 25-00066-UT Final Order (Cert. ¶¶ 79–83).
       Staff takes exception to the statement that Staff’s argument rests on “Staff’s

reading, in isolation, of a single bullet point” of the Case No. 25-00066-UT Final Order (¶

79). Staff further excepts to the statements that Staff argued the Final Order “precluded

SPS from utilizing a future test year period, in all rate cases” and “essentially replaces

17.1.3.9 NMAC” (¶ 83). These paragraphs misstate Staff’s argument, and the Case No.

25-00066-UT Final Order language the Certification quotes supports Staff.

A. Staff relied on three directives, not one bullet point.

        Staff argued that the Final Order reserved general jurisdictional-allocation

determinations “for a future base-rate case on a fully developed evidentiary record,”

required SPS to demonstrate actual use and benefit, and required a methodology that avoids

double-charging and cross-subsidization. Staff stated: “This is the future base-rate case.”

IB 25–27. Staff’s recommendation keeps the FTY for every New Mexico-specific

component. IB 28–29. Staff never argued that the Final Order bars an FTY “in all rate

cases” or displaces 17.1.3 NMAC.

B. The quoted Final Order language in the precedential Case No. 25-00066-UT
supports Staff.
      The Certification quotes ¶ 104 of the Final Order, which declines to approve “a

general jurisdictional allocation methodology at this time.” Cert. ¶ 80. It then concludes

only that Staff did not prove SPS relied on load growth “alone.” Cert. ¶ 82. If the

Commission declined to adopt a general methodology “at this time,” the natural place to

decide it is the next base-rate case on a full record. This is that case. The Certification never

 B. The Certification mischaracterizes Staff’s position.

deficiency that Staff is mostly concerned with.” Cert. ¶ 185 (citing Tr. Vol. IV at 755).

Staff did not oppose the banding methodology; it opposed the rates that methodology

C. The Certification applies the wrong measure to viewing bill impacts.

       SPS and NMLCG relied on comparisons of each class’s increase to the system

average and on the Stipulation’s gradualism adjustments. IB 34–35 (citing Lees Rebuttal

the class percentages needed to change because of its own modifications and answered no

on Mr. Trowbridge’s testimony. Cert. ¶¶ 187–188 & n.231 (citing Tr. Vol. II at 476).

       The Public Utility Act requires service “at fair, just and reasonable rates,” balancing

“the public interest, the interest of consumers and the interest of investors.” NMSA 1978,

§ 62-3-1(B) (quoted at IB 35). Rates may not “unjustly burden ratepayers with excessive

rates.” Coal. for Clean Affordable Energy, 2024-NMSC-016, ¶ 6 (quoted at Cert. ¶ 21).

Both standards look to the rate the customer pays. System-average comparisons and

D. The Certification’s public-interest conclusion has no stated basis.

       The overall determination relies on the negotiated terms “substantially reduc[ing]

SPS’s originally requested rate increase.” Cert. ¶ 396. Simply because the revenue

NMSA 1978, § 62-8-7(A). Distance from a high opening request is an anchoring problem.

It does not show that a 13.6% residential bill increase is just and reasonable.
